title: Bias and Fairness in AI
learning_outcomes: Explain bias and Fairness in AI and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in bias and Fairness in AI to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study bias and Fairness in AI within Responsible AI, Safety, Privacy, and Security. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Responsible AI is a lifecycle practice. Assess foreseeable harms, data handling, security boundaries, transparency needs, and routes for human accountability.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Fairness analysis checks whether errors, access, or outcomes differ across relevant groups and contexts. Group definitions and metrics require domain judgment, and aggregate performance can hide unequal impacts.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Bias in data collection
items.text: Bias in data collection is one of the concepts used to reason about bias and fairness in ai. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Historical and sampling bias
items.text: A sample is the subset of records observed; the population is the group about which a conclusion is intended. Biased or unrepresentative sampling can limit generalization regardless of sample size.

items.title: Fairness metrics and trade-offs
items.text: Fairness evaluation compares relevant errors, access, or outcomes across groups and contexts. No single metric resolves every normative trade-off, so justify subgroup choices and report limitations.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what bias and fairness in ai takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. Read the example before running it and predict the output. 3. Run the small example, compare actual and expected output, then change one input or assumption and repeat. 4. Record what the example demonstrates and what it does not demonstrate about a real system.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with the task definition and the inputs available. Make the expected behavior explicit, choose a simple reference point, and inspect both ordinary examples and cases where assumptions may fail. Responsible AI is a lifecycle practice. Assess foreseeable harms, data handling, security boundaries, transparency needs, and routes for human accountability.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step

content.task: Try it yourself: complete a small risk review for bias and fairness in ai. Identify affected people, plausible failure modes, evidence needed, preventative controls, a residual risk, and the owner who would review the control after a change. The linked practice activity is: Fairness Assessment.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.
If output differs, restore the original input and compare one changed value at a time.
If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
These examples require no external packages, network access, model credentials, or personal data.
